title: Finding Acquisition Targets
answer: Finding acquisition targets is the front end of private equity and corporate development work: the search for companies worth buying, before any valuation, diligence or negotiation begins. In an AI context the scope widens to include not just operating businesses but also teams, model weights, data sets and tooling that a buyer may want to fold into an existing platform. The output of the exercise is a shortlist, ranked and reasoned, that a deal team can take into first contact. It is a screening discipline, not a decision, and it sits upstream of everything that costs real money.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Finding acquisition targets is the front end of private equity and corporate development work: the search for companies worth buying, before any valuation, diligence or negotiation begins. In an AI context the scope widens to include not just operating businesses but also teams, model weights, data sets and tooling that a buyer may want to fold into an existing platform. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The raw material is company and market data: registries, filings, funding announcements, patent records, job postings, product pages and news. On this site that kind of material is represented by 514 company pages and 401 merger and acquisition filings, alongside 117 listed AI-related instruments with daily prices where a target or a comparable is publicly traded. Practitioners typically assemble a working universe in a spreadsheet or a CRM, then enrich it with scraped and licensed feeds. The infrastructure question is less about compute and more about how fresh, deduplicated and traceable the underlying records are.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The traditional method is a thesis first: define the segment, the size band, the capability gap and the geography, then build a long list and filter it down. AI changes the speed of the long list, not the logic of the filter. Language models can read filings, transcripts and product documentation at volume, cluster companies by what they actually do rather than by their self-description, and surface candidates that keyword screens miss. A human still sets the criteria, checks the evidence and decides which names are worth a call. The failure mode is a confident shortlist built on stale or misread data, so every candidate needs a source a colleague can open.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Deal sourcing runs on confidential information, and the rules that matter are the ones about how it is handled. Material non-public information, insider trading restrictions, market abuse rules and the terms of any data licence all constrain what can be collected, stored and acted on. On the AI side, using scraped personal data or copyrighted material to train or prompt a screening tool raises questions under privacy and data protection law, and the site's 229 compliance and regulation pages and 150 active AI lawsuits show how live those questions are. Provenance matters: a shortlist should record where each fact came from and when it was retrieved. Nothing here is legal advice, and a deal team should route these questions to counsel.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward continuous, always-on sourcing rather than periodic campaigns. As more company data becomes machine readable, the screening step compresses, and the scarce skills shift to judgement about fit, timing and price. Buyers are also getting more explicit about AI assets themselves, which means target lists increasingly mix conventional businesses with teams and models. Expect more scrutiny of how these tools are built and fed, and more demand for audit trails behind any recommendation. The tooling will keep improving, but the discipline of knowing why a target is on the list will remain the part that decides whether a deal is worth doing.
